researchUpdates.title: Machine learning-based prediction of 90-day tensile strength in geopolymer concrete under varying input-variable scenarios
researchUpdates.authors: Parnian Mehravar, Hossein Bahrami and Hamidreza Ghazvinian
researchUpdates.summary: Four machine-learning approaches are compared across eleven input-variable scenarios for predicting one reported endpoint: 90-day tensile strength of geopolymer concrete.
highlights: The scenario design tests how prediction changes when different subsets of mixture and processing descriptors are available.
The target is specifically 90-day tensile strength; it is not evidence for compressive, flexural or shear performance.
researchUpdates.access: Publisher-accessible early-version evidence. Model performance is dataset-specific and still requires independent external validation, uncertainty reporting and checks against new precursor sources and laboratories.

researchUpdates.title: Precursor Compatibility in Multi-Source Alkali-Activated Materials: Coupled Dissolution, Elemental Competition, and Phase Selection
researchUpdates.authors: Rui Wang, Xiaodong Li, Zhenzhen Jiao, Huanming Zhang, Guofeng Xue, Zhixiong Lu, Yiqi Wang, Qi Zhang and Ruyi Yan
researchUpdates.summary: This review organizes multi-precursor alkali activation around interacting dissolution rates, competition among released species and the resulting selection of reaction products.
highlights: Compatibility is framed as a conditional window controlled by source chemistry and activation conditions, not as a permanent label attached to a waste stream.
The review connects precursor interactions to phase development, offering a stronger screening logic than comparing bulk oxide totals alone.
researchUpdates.access: Review-level synthesis rather than new experimental replication. Its organizing framework does not replace source-specific characterization, mixture trials, durability testing or local availability and safety assessments.

researchUpdates.title: Waste-to-resource geopolymer technology: mechanical, durability, and microstructural performance of red Mud–fly ash-stabilized black cotton soil
researchUpdates.authors: Rohit Raj, Brahmdeo Yadav, Sumit Kumar and Ashok Kumar Yadav
researchUpdates.summary: Red mud and fly ash are assessed as an alkali-activated stabilizing system for expansive black cotton soil using mechanical, durability and microstructural observations.
highlights: The study evaluates a soil-treatment application, so binder behavior is interpreted within a mineral-rich soil matrix rather than as standalone concrete.
Combining performance tests with microstructural observations helps relate stabilization behavior to the tested red-mud, fly-ash and soil system.
researchUpdates.access: Publisher-accessible early-version evidence. Results remain tied to the sampled soil, residue chemistry, activator, curing and laboratory protocols; they do not establish field service life or independent replication.

researchUpdates.title: Machine Learning and Life Cycle Assessment for Geopolymer Construction Materials: From Precursor Variability to Scalable Low-Carbon Deployment
researchUpdates.authors: Justin Kinda, Tégawendé Justin Zaida, Etienne Malbila and Fati Zoma
researchUpdates.summary: This critical review examines how machine learning, life-cycle assessment and multi-objective decision methods can be connected when designing geopolymer construction materials under variable precursor supply.
highlights: The review treats precursor variability and deployment scale as constraints that must travel with model predictions and environmental comparisons.
It links performance prediction with life-cycle objectives instead of assuming that a mechanically acceptable mixture is automatically the lowest-impact option.
researchUpdates.access: Pre-proof review evidence. The proposed integration is a synthesis, not a validated universal workflow; life-cycle conclusions depend on geography, system boundary, inventory quality and energy and transport assumptions.

researchUpdates.title: Interpretable machine learning and experimental validation for predicting the mechanical performance of geopolymer concrete with and without fiber reinforcement
researchUpdates.authors: Not independently verified from accessible publisher metadata
researchUpdates.summary: An interpretable machine-learning workflow compares mechanical-property prediction for geopolymer concrete datasets with and without fiber reinforcement and includes experimental validation.
highlights: Separating fiber-reinforced from unreinforced cases makes reinforcement state an explicit model-domain boundary.
The work addresses compressive strength, elastic modulus and flexural strength as distinct targets rather than treating one property as a proxy for the others.
researchUpdates.access: Publisher abstract-level evidence only. The accessible record did not expose a verifiable author list or full validation design; reported model behavior should not be generalized across laboratories, fibers, precursors or untested properties.

journalArticle.title: A prediction needs a domain boundary
journalArticle.summary: New studies on machine learning, precursor compatibility and deployment show that useful digital guidance begins by stating where a result applies.
paragraphs: Three of this week’s records use or review machine learning, but none supports a property-agnostic predictor. Tensile strength, compressive strength, elastic modulus and flexural strength remain separate endpoints, and reinforcement state changes the model domain.

The chemistry review adds the material-side boundary: multi-source precursors interact through dissolution, elemental competition and phase selection. A model trained on one set of residues cannot treat a new source as equivalent merely because its broad material label matches.

For a formulation advisor, each prediction should therefore carry its target property, age, reinforcement state, precursor provenance, curing regime, application and validation domain. Life-cycle claims also need geography and system boundaries. These records guide database design; they do not independently replicate one another or validate user mixtures.
